lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.unitTitle: Measurement: Time, Liquid Volume, and Mass
lessonRef.focus: choosing a unit and estimating before measuring
lessonRef.title: Concept extension: choosing a unit and estimating before measuring

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: This example applies the idea in a new setting. Notice what stayed the same.

items.prompt: A jug has 350 milliliters. Another 120 milliliters are poured in. How much is in the jug now?

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Talk through what is different about this case before you start.

items.prompt: A container has 138 milliliters. 101 milliliters are removed. How many milliliters are left?
A container has 374 grams. Another 285 grams are poured in. How many grams are in the container now?

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A container has 89 liters. Another 137 liters are poured in. How many liters are in the container now?
A container has 295 kilograms. 95 kilograms are removed. How many kilograms are left?
A container has 314 liters. 99 liters are removed. How many liters are left?
A container has 569 grams. Another 141 grams are poured in. How many grams are in the container now?

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Explain, in writing, what made this case different from the original one.

items.prompt: A container has 274 milliliters. 61 milliliters are removed. How many milliliters are left?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: A container has 588 milliliters. Another 211 milliliters are poured in. How many milliliters are in the container now?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
